title.narrative: Community beekeeping for conservation and empowerment in Kibondo, Tanzania

description.narrative: Tanzania suffers from one of the highest rates of deforestation, a decrease of 1.1% per year of the total forested area, caused by unsustainable demand and use of charcoal and the expansion of farming land into forest areas. Sustainable beekeeping could offer a solution for this, yet most smallholder beekeepers in Tanzania live in poverty, lack access to markets and skills and technology to produce high quality honey for exports and have a critical position in the honey value chain, despite the growing demand for honey in Europe due to the declining honeybee colonies. Dutch company Jasmine Bee B.V. wants to contribute to stop non-sustainable land-use practices and converse the environment by developing an organic certified commercial beekeeping supply chain in Tanzania that depends on the vitality of the forest and thus will encourage rural communities to protect their environment. To prepare for future investments, demonstrate commercial viability of organic honey from Tanzania and to have an immediate positive impact on the local community, Technical Assistance (DGGF) provided support to Jasmine Bee and its local subsidiary in Tanzania. The project included setting up partnerships with local authorities and secure community involvement to develop a local supply chain, implementing an Internal Control System for organic certification to meet European market requirements, transfer of knowledge regarding forest preservation, organic beekeeping and good agricultural and food processing practices, the set-up of 3 honey collection and processing facilities, providing local smallholder beekeepers with training, permits and protective clothes to improve working conditions and pre-financing the first container shipment to Europe. The project was successful and supported 20 FTE direct jobs, of which 12 FTE include 36, mostly female, seasonal processing workers during harvest seasons. The project also supported 979 indirect jobs and provided sustainable knowledge transfer to 2117 people. In total, 2117 smallholder beekeepers received training, of which 949 are now organic certified and were able to sell their honey for the European market. Jasmine Bee is now looking to expand its activities in Tanzania which will likely result in an additional 500 smallholder beekeepers being trained and certified which allows them to sell their honey to the European market and will contribute to sustainable agricultural practices, improved livelihoods of beekeepers involved and will have a positive impact on forest and wildlife preservation in general.
